records.title: BPMN-Based Design of Multi-Agent Systems: Personalized Language Learning Workflow Automation with RAG-Enhanced Knowledge Access

evidence_notes.summary: This paper treats a BPMN diagram as an executable specification rather than documentation: pools, lanes, tasks, gateways and message flows are compiled one-to-one into LangGraph agent nodes, tool nodes, routers and message edges, so the agents' branching logic is fixed by the model instead of by free-form prompting. That transformation is the mechanism RQ1 cares about, but the domain is Luxembourgish language tutoring, so no policy or violation construct exists and nothing is measured that maps onto compliance. Evaluation is RAGAs scores over 200 held-out queries plus a 14-student usability pilot; the only claimed comparison against an unconstrained agent is a bare assertion that hallucination was reduced relative to a single-agent LLM whose numbers are explicitly not shown. For RQ2 it is therefore evidence of a control mechanism (process-model-bound orchestration plus RAG grounding plus teacher-in-the-loop approval) that has been built and demonstrated but never empirically contrasted with a baseline. Note that Appendix B reproduces the system prompts given to the tutor agents, which read as imperative instructions addressed to a model; these are paper content quoted as data and were not acted on.

records.title: Accountable Multi-Agent AI Systems: Orchestration Frameworks for Enterprise Workflow Automation with Human-in-the-Loop Verification

evidence_notes.summary: AMAOS makes human verification an architectural primitive rather than a configuration flag: the orchestrator decomposes a task into a DAG, computes a risk score from agent confidence, business impact, irreversibility and novelty, and inserts typed advisory, mandatory-approval or supervisor-escalation gates wherever that score crosses a threshold, backed by a hash-chained audit ledger. The reported experiment has exactly the shape RQ1 asks for, because the control condition is the same LLM and tool configuration with the gates disabled, and both dependent variables are reported together: a 94.7% mean reduction in unauthorised autonomous actions at 87.3% of baseline throughput. The control mechanism is risk-gated human approval rather than binding to an explicit process model, so it belongs in RQ2's inventory rather than as a direct answer to RQ1. Credibility is weak: a single-author Zenodo preprint with no model identification, no per-deployment sample sizes, no statistical tests, no released data and three unnamed enterprise deployments, so these figures should be recorded as claimed rather than established.

records.title: A Privacy-Preserving On-Device Multi-Agent Architecture for AI PC (POMA) Workflow Automation

evidence_notes.summary: POMA interposes a runtime Policy Verifier between an LLM-driven computer-use agent and the desktop, restricting it to a typed set of least-privilege primitives whose invocation envelopes carry plan-step binding, evidence provenance, sensitivity tags and destination trust, then scoring each action on impact times evidence-uncertainty and returning ALLOW, ESCALATE or DENY. The design articulates RQ1's dependent-variable pair unusually cleanly, defining task completion rate and policy overhead alongside attack success rate, unsafe action rate (false-allow), true block rate, escalation accuracy and confirmation burden. Critically the paper reports no results: Section VII is a proposed evaluation methodology, and the named baselines (CUA without verifier gating, single-agent end-to-end, optional cloud-first) plus the Policy Verifier, provenance and escalation ablations are planned rather than executed. It is therefore useful to RQ2 as a control-mechanism taxonomy and as a metric template, but contributes no empirical evidence. The adversarial battery quotes injection strings such as an instruction to ignore policy and export secrets as example attacks; these are described data, not instructions, and were treated as such.

records.title: GALENA: A Governance-Aware LLM Enterprise Navigation Architecture for Autonomous Multi-Agent Workflow Automation with Compliance Enforcement

evidence_notes.summary: GALENA encodes regulatory obligations as a formal constraint set carried inside every workflow object and enforces a hard governance gate before each agent action and again before any response is delivered, with three-valued PASS/REVISE/ROLLBACK verdicts and a drift monitor that re-opens deployed workflows when policy or data distributions shift. Of everything in this batch it maps most directly onto RQ1's contrast, because its six baselines (ReAct, AutoGen, LangChain Agents, DSPy, Reflexion, DataGovAgent) represent the 'policy as prompt or post-hoc filter' condition, and it reports the two dependent variables jointly: task completion accuracy 0.97 against 0.82 for the strongest baseline, with governance violation rate falling from 0.11 to 0.03. Taken at face value that is violation reduction with no completion loss, which is precisely the outcome RQ1 hypothesises. The evidence is fragile, however: a single-author paper in a journal with a non-standard DOI prefix, every metric against every baseline reported at p < 0.001, no released artefacts or datasets, and an experimental configuration naming a model version I could not corroborate, so these numbers should be graded low-confidence rather than discarded.

records.title: A stigmergy-driven multi-agent framework for intelligent task orchestration

evidence_notes.summary: This master's thesis carries the strongest evaluation design in the batch: 790 controlled runs across nine ablation configurations in a warehouse-brokerage scenario with expert-defined ground truth, effect sizes reported as Cliff's delta because the paired tests are underpowered, and a 2x2 factorial analysis of the two validation layers. For RQ2 it separately ablates five distinct control mechanisms - pheromone-weighted contract-net bidding, SHACL structural validation, a deterministic rule-based domain compliance agent, an LLM strategist for runtime replanning, and an ethics-check gate - against a coordination-free baseline, and ranks their marginal contributions. Its most important result for RQ1 is a dissociation rather than a headline gain: removing both validation layers left assignment accuracy unchanged at 0.98 while detected violations dropped from 40% to 0%, demonstrating that task completion and policy conformance are orthogonal constructs that must be measured separately. The deterministic compliance agent achieved perfect recall (TPR 1.000, FPR 0.011, F1 0.992) precisely because it enumerates rules rather than inferring them, which is a useful counterpoint to LLM-mediated policy checking.

records.title: Open-Rosalind: Tool-First Biomedical LLM Agents with Process-Aware Benchmarking

evidence_notes.summary: This is the most directly informative study in the batch for RQ1 because it isolates the constraint itself as an experimental variable. Open-Rosalind binds the agent to pre-declared workflow templates under a hard step bound with mandatory tool mediation and mandatory traces, then ablates each constraint separately (full, react, no_tool, no_cite, no_template) over 1,770 runs across six model families with paired seed replications. The results cut against a simple 'constraints help' reading: removing the templated workflow barely moved accuracy (81.4% to 80.5%), the tool-first constraint carried almost all the gain (81.4% to 57.3%), and against a free-form ReAct baseline the constrained pipeline only won decisively where the model was weak at unconstrained tool use, while being statistically indistinguishable on the deployment model. An author-independent hold-out then collapsed the constrained pipeline below both ReAct and the no-tool condition, and it only partially recovered after routing repairs, which is direct evidence that measured benefits of process constraints are contingent on routing robustness and tool coverage rather than intrinsic. Its explicit diagnosis-and-repair reporting is also a methodological template worth carrying into this review's own comparison design.

records.title: Context is key for cybersecurity: leveraging external knowledge for process model explanation via LLMs

evidence_notes.summary: This peer-reviewed study runs RQ1's relationship in the opposite direction: instead of constraining an agent with a process model, it hands a BPMN model plus an unstructured standard to an LLM and measures how well the model can decide compliance. Across two real-world cases (an ISO 27001 incident-response process and a SIREN-annotated IEC 62443-3-3 production process) it shows that supplying the standard as explicit context lifts accuracy from 49.3% with no context to 74.6% with context plus few-shot examples, quantifying how much policy adherence is recoverable from natural-language instruction alone. Its most transferable contribution is a four-part error typology over the incorrect answers, in which reasoning failures (49) and context-retrieval failures (23) dominate while outright hallucination occurs twice, reframing the compliance bottleneck away from fabrication and toward mapping structured process semantics onto unstructured rules. It also documents a measurement threat directly relevant to this review: the automated LLM judge penalised valid alternate reasoning paths and agreed with human raters only fairly (Cohen's kappa 0.3909). One internal inconsistency worth flagging is that the results section counts 12 input-interpretation failures across 86 non-correct instances while the discussion reports 4 across 78.

records.title: E2E Process Automation Leveraging Generative AI and IDP-Based Automation Agent: A Case Study on Corporate Expense Processing

evidence_notes.summary: This is an industrial deployment report from Samsung SDS describing a four-stage expense-processing pipeline in which an explicit policy database, not the language model, carries the compliance decision on the routine path. IDP extracts receipt fields, a whitelist/blacklist policy database performs the first classification, and the LLM is invoked only for unclassified or ambiguous items where it produces an advisory account recommendation with a stated rationale; a finance officer makes the binding decision, which is then written back into the policy database so the same item is handled deterministically next time. For RQ2 that is a concrete hybrid control mechanism - deterministic rules for the covered space, LLM advice plus human ratification for the residue, with the human decision persisted as new policy - deployed at production scale rather than simulated. Evidentially it is thin: the only measurement is a confusion matrix over 1,448 receipts (accuracy 0.83, precision 1.00, recall 0.82, F1 0.90), there is no baseline arm, and the widely quoted 80-90% time saving is explicitly presented as an expected effect derived from general adoption cases rather than a measured before-and-after comparison.

records.title: CAPRI: A Context-Aware Privacy Framework for Multi-Agent Generative AI Applications

evidence_notes.summary: CAPRI inserts a local 'gatekeeper' LLM between an enterprise and a cloud LLM agent, converting user input into typed entity structures whose PII values are contextually pseudonymized and reversibly mapped via UUIDs before a ReAct agent reasons over them. Its relevance to RQ1 is indirect but structurally analogous: it measures what happens to task completion when an agent is forced to operate over a constrained, structured representation instead of raw natural-language input. The finding is a graded utility cost - imposing entity structure alone improved task success and reduced turns relative to an unconstrained ReAct baseline, whereas heavy pseudonymization degraded success sharply because referential integrity broke inside reasoning traces. For RQ2 it contributes an empirically evaluated control mechanism (local pre-processing gate plus reversible mapping) benchmarked against an unmodified ToolEmu ReAct prompt. The paper reports no compliance or violation metric at all, only task success and turn counts, so it speaks to the 'task completion' side of RQ1 rather than the 'policy violation' side.

quotes.text: The entity-only configuration improved the success rate by 4% and reduced the number of conversational turns by 1.3 compared to the baseline.
As shown in Table 1, this configuration outperformed the fully pseudonymized approach, achieving a 56% success rate while reducing the number of conversational turns by 1.1 compared to the baseline.
Although the integration of entity structures into user queries yielded improvements, the overall success rate for all four (4) configurations remained limited to a maximum of 64%.

extraction.baseline: LLM agents running an out-of-the-box ToolEmu ReAct prompt on unmodified tool definitions with no entity structures and no pseudonymization

records.title: Retail Resilience Engine: An Agentic AI Framework for Building Reliable Retail Systems With Test-Driven Development Approach

evidence_notes.summary: This paper proposes the Retail Resilience Engine, a layered agentic-AI framework that fine-tunes a transformer on retail and test-driven-development corpora and wraps it in a keyword-similarity prompt filter plus a test-first validation loop. Its contribution to RQ2 is a control mechanism of a different kind from formal constraints: generated test cases and pass/fail gates used as the reliability mechanism, evaluated against a human-expert baseline rather than against another agent configuration. For RQ1 the evidence is weak - there is no policy, no violation metric and no compliance-critical process; the reported outcome is decision agreement with experts and plan-quality scores. Reported numbers are internally inconsistent (the abstract and conclusion claim a 97.5% similarity index while the body reports a Pearson correlation of 0.96, and filtering accuracy is given as 98.2%, 98.20% and 98.22% in different places), which should be weighed when citing it. Evaluation samples are very small (ten queries for the alignment experiment, ten domains for robustness).

quotes.text: The ρ is 0.96, which means that the decision made by the proposed system is 96% similar to the decision made by human specialists.
The proposed RRE achieved a total score of 13 out of 15, on par with Expert 3 and only slightly below Expert 1.
While the engine performs well across various retail domains, its effectiveness is currently limited to predefined categories such as inventory management and demand forecasting.

extraction.framework: Retail Resilience Engine (RRE)
extraction.topology: single-agent layered pipeline (data source, pre-processing, feature management, software layer with AI Agent API and Application Control Unit); the paper frames this as replacing multi-level human decision-making with single-point agentic decision-making
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a proprietary corpus of 100,000 documents (5,000 customer reviews, 10,000 inventory records, 50,000 operational-log documents, 35,000 analytics/system-log documents), with 10 retail queries for the alignment experiment, 100/500/1000-query scalability sets, 10 retail domains for robustness, and 5 filtering experiments
extraction.baseline: Human experts with more than 10 years of experience in retail system development, used both for decision-impact ratings and for implementation-plan quality scoring
extraction.key_results: Retail Decision Impact Alignment Pearson correlation rho = 0.96 (abstract and conclusion instead state a 97.5% similarity index); paired t-test p = 0.021 against alpha = 0.05; implementation plan quality 13 out of 15 versus experts; average prompt-filtering accuracy reported as 98.20% (and as 98.22% elsewhere in the text); accuracy above 90% across all ten tested retail domains; 52 ms average inference per query and 4.2 GB memory on an NVIDIA A100.
extraction.limitations: Authors state ethical and data-privacy exposure from PII in training data with no federated learning or differential privacy yet; effectiveness limited to predefined retail categories; the engine operates as a black box with no explainability; real-time scalability requires further optimization; hyperparameters were set heuristically rather than optimized; centralized cloud-only design; decision latency, unpredictable market conditions, and dependence on high-quality input data are named as agentic-AI challenges.

records.title: Solver-Aided Verification of Policy Compliance in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This is the most direct RQ1 test in this batch: the same airline operational policy is given to one agent as a natural-language policy document in context and to another as SMT-LIB-2.0 constraints checked by Z3 as a pre-condition on every planned tool call, with blocked calls returned to the agent alongside a minimum unsatisfiable core for replanning. The result is a precision/recall trade-off rather than a free lunch - invalid write tool calls fell to 29% of write calls while the fraction of correct write calls also fell, yet end-to-end pass^k task success did not degrade and in fact improved slightly and was more consistent across repeated trials. For RQ2 the paper also supplies a rare negative result on the upstream translation step: four successive designs for compiling natural-language policy into logic all failed on syntactic correctness, semantic completeness or constraint tightness until manual review and tuning were added. That makes the reported compliance gain contingent on human-curated encodings rather than on automated policy compilation.

quotes.text: However, prompt-based guidance does not provide reliable policy enforcement. As policies grow longer and more complex, purely prompt-based enforcement becomes increasingly brittle and harder to validate.

While the baseline produced a roughly equal proportion of valid and invalid write tool calls, theTaLLMwith policy checker reduced the fraction of invalid write tool calls to29%(measured over all write tool calls).
Overall, both achieve similar success rates, with the policy checker yielding a slight improvement.

extraction.topology: single-agent tool-planning loop with an external runtime gate that intercepts each candidate tool call, checks it against an SMT policy encoding via Z3, and prompts replanning (bounded to three attempts) on UNSAT
extraction.benchmark: tau2-bench (tau2-verified lineage), airline domain only: 50 tasks, 13 tools, and a 1242-word policy document; 4 trials per task with pass^k reporting; GPT-4.1 as customer and service agent, GPT-4o for tool-call validation
extraction.baseline: The same tool-augmented LLM agent with the natural-language policy document supplied in context and no solver-aided checking (prompt-based policy steering)
extraction.key_results: Invalid write tool calls fell to 29% of all write tool calls under solver-aided checking versus a roughly equal valid/invalid split for the baseline; write-call precision and recall shifted from 0.51/0.61 (baseline) to 0.70/0.49 (solver-aided); pass^1 through pass^4 were 0.560, 0.433, 0.375, 0.340 for the baseline versus 0.625, 0.543, 0.495, 0.460 for the solver-aided agent; success rate decreased by only 26% as k increased versus 40% for the baseline.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that automatically translating natural-language policies into logical constraints is challenging and that verifying semantic completeness requires manual review, so policy encodings are treated as explicit human-reviewed artifacts rather than fully automated output; three recurring failure classes are named (syntactic correctness, semantic completeness, constraint tightness); the solver-aided agent produces fewer correct write tool calls than the baseline; only the airline domain of the benchmark was evaluated; only tool-use policies are covered, excluding behavioural policies such as information-disclosure and confirmation rules.

records.title: Compliance Digital Twins for Autonomous Financial Agents: Reliability-Aware Scenario Assurance via Calibrated LLM Evaluation

evidence_notes.summary: The Compliance Digital Twin proposes a synchronized machine-readable model of financial process graphs, control mappings, segregation-of-duties rules and IAM entitlements, against which agents are exercised on injected routine, degraded and adversarial scenarios before deployment. Two elements matter for RQ1: the explicit process model (process graphs with decision points, handoffs and exception paths) is the normative baseline against which agent behaviour is judged, and a reliability-aware control layer converts an estimated violation risk into a three-level autonomy policy (autonomous, supervised, human-gated) with default thresholds of 0.35 and 0.65. For RQ2 the evaluated control mechanism is pre-deployment scenario assurance plus a calibrated LLM judge, benchmarked against a conventional test suite. The central caveat is that the agents were not real LLM agents: agent behaviour was a probabilistic but scripted decision model, so the reported detection gains are properties of the assurance harness rather than evidence about how LLM agents behave under process constraints. The paper also reports the conventional baseline detection rate as 43% in the text and 47% in the per-family table.

quotes.text: The CDT detected 89% of injected compliance violations and authorization failures before simulated deployment, compared with 43% for the conventional test suite, a 46 percentage -point improvement.
SoD enforcement efficacy reached 96% across the 30 injected toxic entitlement scenarios
These results are reported for a controlled simulation on a single synthetic workflow and should be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive.

extraction.framework: Compliance Digital Twin (CDT)
extraction.topology: three-agent pipeline (document-interpretation, approval-routing, payment-release) under a reliability-aware supervisory control layer that modulates autonomy between autonomous, supervised and human-gated modes
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a synthetic invoice-to-payment (accounts payable) workflow with 150 parameterized scenario instances across five scenario families (30 per family), four SOX-aligned approval tiers, six SoD constraints and eight role-entitlement mappings; ground truth for the 30 adversarial instances set by three domain experts with Cohen's kappa = 0.84
extraction.baseline: A conventional pre-deployment test suite of 47 unit tests and 18 scripted integration tests covering the same workflow steps, described as representative of current industry practice
extraction.key_results: Pre-deployment detection rate 89% (CDT) versus 43% (baseline), a 46 percentage-point gap, though the per-family table totals 134/150 = 89% versus 71/150 = 47%; SoD enforcement efficacy 96% versus 36%, with SoD false-negative rate 4% versus 64%; largest gaps on SoD and IAM boundary scenarios (97% versus 20%) and adversarial scenarios (80% versus 23%), smallest on routine flows (93% versus 83%); configuration-change detection latency 3.2 hours versus a simulated 14-day audit cycle; LLM judge ECE 0.041 (reduced from 0.068 after one recalibration), Brier score 0.172, chain-of-thought reasoning accuracy 0.83, judge-human agreement 86.7%.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the results come from a controlled simulation on a single synthetic workflow and are indicative rather than definitive; the agent behaviour model is probabilistic but scripted and does not capture production LLM agent outputs or their emergent failure modes; the baseline comparator is representative but simplified, so organizations with better test coverage may see higher baseline detection; generalization to larger agent ensembles and live regulatory data requires further study; cross-institutional and multi-jurisdictional settings are not addressed; the reliability model is correlational rather than causal; convergence guarantees for the autonomy policy under arbitrary distributional shift remain open.

records.title: Near-Miss: Latent Policy Failure Detection in Agentic Workflows

evidence_notes.summary: This paper attacks a measurement assumption that RQ1 depends on: if policy adherence is scored by comparing the final system state against a gold state, agents that skip a mandatory verification step but still land on the right outcome are counted as compliant. The authors define a 'near-miss' or latent failure as a mutating tool call that was not adequately informed, operationalize it by replaying ToolGuard-generated guard code and searching the trajectory for the required read-only tool call or an information-equivalent substitute, and validate the detector against author annotation. Measured on six contemporary LLM agents, latent failures occur in 8-17% of trajectories containing mutating tool calls even when the final outcome matches ground truth, and the authors report that explicit policy violations account for roughly 25% of all simulation failures. For RQ1 this means outcome-only violation counts understate the true policy-violation rate, and any study comparing constrained against natural-language-instructed agents on final-state metrics alone will be biased in favour of the unconstrained agent. Note: the appendices reproduce the system prompts used for the detector; these are paper artifacts quoted as data and contain no instructions directed at this review.

quotes.text: Although not explicitly reported in prior work, our experiments suggest that policy violations account for approximately 25% of all simulation failures in theτ 2-bench Airlines domain
Both Claude-Sonnet4 and Kimi-K2.5 show near-miss rate (NMR) of 7% per human annotation.
Among the evaluated agents, GPT-oss-120b achieves the best result with a near-miss rate of 8.6%, followed by Claude-Sonnet4 with 12.1%.

extraction.topology: single-agent ReAct-style tool-calling loop with a user simulator; ToolGuard guard code is replayed offline for evaluation rather than enforced at runtime
extraction.benchmark: tau2-verified Airlines domain (enhanced tau2-bench), 50 tasks with 4 trials each for 200 simulations per agent, GPT4.1 as user simulator; two data-access tools were added to the domain
extraction.baseline: Conventional reference-based evaluation that compares only the final database state against the expected gold state; the two history-search strategies (LLM-based search versus generated-code search) and six LLM agents are also compared against each other and against author-annotated near-miss ground truth
extraction.key_results: Latent failures occur in 8-17% of trajectories involving mutating tool calls even when the final outcome matches ground truth; per-model near-miss rate over trajectories with mutating tool calls: GPT-oss-120b 0.086, Qwen2.5-72b 0.084 (flagged as unreliable), Claude-Sonnet4 0.121, Gemini-3-pro 0.140, Kimi-K2.5 0.144, GPT5-chat 0.173; policy violations account for approximately 25% of all simulation failures; human-annotated near-miss rate was 7% for both Claude-Sonnet4 and Kimi-K2.5; generated-code search with Claude-Sonnet4 achieved precision 1.00 and recall 1.00 on both agents; no clear relationship emerged between the policy-violation ratio and the near-miss ratio; update_reservation_flights was the mutating tool most often invoked without checks and get_flight_status the most frequently bypassed read-only tool.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the approach is bounded by the quality of ToolGuard-generated guard code, since errors or omissions in the LLM-generated guards directly reduce detection accuracy; the pipeline adds computational overhead (extra LLM calls per trajectory and tool invocation for the LLM-based variant); ToolGuard is used only for offline evaluation rather than runtime enforcement; evaluation covers a single benchmark with a limited set of tools and policies, and the authors call for validation on additional domains and larger, more diverse settings; annotation was done by the authors rather than independent annotators.

records.title: From Business Events to Auditable Decisions: Ontology-Governed Graph Simulation for Enterprise AI

evidence_notes.summary: LOM-action argues explicitly against the natural-language-instruction arm of RQ1: business scenario conditions injected as prompt instructions are treated by the model as soft preferences, so it may still act on the unrestricted graph. The proposed alternative binds the agent to a mandatory three-phase pipeline (scenario parsing, sandbox graph mutation, decision derivation on the evolved graph) with every mutation logged for auditor replay. The paper's most transferable contribution for RQ2 is a measurement idea: it separates answer accuracy from tool-chain F1 and defines an 'illusive accuracy' index as their difference, showing frontier baselines reaching about 80% accuracy while recording F1 of 0.00 on basic traversal tasks because they answered from parametric knowledge without ever touching the sandbox. On the scenario-constrained tasks, where the constrained graph genuinely differs from the static one, baseline accuracy also collapsed to 0.64-0.66 against 1.00. The comparison is confounded, which the authors concede: LOM-action is fine-tuned while the baselines are zero-shot, and the controlled ablation (same fine-tuning without the simulation curriculum) is not run.

extraction.topology: single-agent dual-mode execution (skill mode for registered skill-ontology tool calls, reasoning mode for novel in-context computation) over an isolated graph_id-keyed sandbox, with a LOM-as-Judge step re-grounding outputs from delegated frontier models
extraction.benchmark: LOM-action benchmark: 11 function-calling tasks over a 19-function graph API suite on synthetic Neo4j subgraphs of 20-30 nodes and 30-60 edges, 200 training and 100 held-out test samples per task (2,200 train / 1,100 test) with disjoint graph UUIDs
extraction.baseline: Zero-shot frontier LLMs Doubao-1.8 and DeepSeek-V3.2 invoked through their native function-calling APIs with the full 19-function schema, means over three independent runs
extraction.key_results: Overall answer accuracy 93.82% (LOM-action) versus 80.00% (Doubao-1.8) and 80.18% (DeepSeek-V3.2); overall tool-chain F1 98.74% versus 24.42% and 36.21%; illusive accuracy index 0.56, 0.44 and -0.05 respectively; F1 = 0.00 for both baselines on all four basic traversal tasks despite near-perfect accuracy; on fc_constraint_connection accuracy 1.00 versus 0.66 and 0.64, a 34-point gap, with baseline F1 of 0.325 and 0.351; on the hybrid coloring task LOM-action F1 = 1.00 with accuracy 0.46; manual inspection of 50 Doubao-1.8 CONNECTIVITY outputs found 47 correct answers produced with zero tool calls and 3 malformed calls; LOM-action error mix: 47% in-context computation, 29% incomplete tool chain, 15% argument hallucination, 9% mode misclassification.
extraction.limitations: Authors state all experiments use synthetic Neo4j subgraphs of 20-30 nodes and 30-60 edges, far below real enterprise ontology scale, with no demonstration of cross-scale or cross-domain transfer; the fine-tuned versus zero-shot comparison does not isolate architectural contribution from training contribution and the controlled ablation (a Qwen3.5-27B fine-tuned without the Phase 2 simulation curriculum) has not been run; end-to-end latency, throughput and concurrent-event sandbox locking are unmeasured; scenario conditions are currently stated in event payload text rather than derived from ontology traversal; Task 11 is a graph-theoretic task whose enterprise connection is illustrative rather than grounded in a deployed process.

records.title: Provably Secure Agent Guardrail

evidence_notes.summary: The ePCA framework refuses natural-language intent at the enforcement boundary: agents must serialize each action into a strongly typed payload that is deterministically compiled into first-order logic and checked by an SMT solver against hard-coded safety axioms, so unsafe transitions become UNSAT rather than blocked by judgement. For RQ2 the useful part is the head-to-head against the two control mechanisms practitioners actually deploy - stateless attribute-based access control and LLM-as-a-Judge - on a multi-step financial transfer task with time-segmentation and meta-rule attacks. ABAC failed by under-blocking because it evaluates steps in isolation, the LLM judge was unstable across models, and ePCA blocked all adversarial trajectories while accepting benign ones at 0.44 ms average verification latency versus roughly 15 seconds for the judge. The authors are unusually explicit that this is a mechanism demonstration rather than a statistical benchmark, and that the guarantee is only as complete as the hand-written axiom set, which is the key qualification for RQ1: it proves absence of violations of declared axioms, not absence of unsafe behaviour.

quotes.text: In the Multi-Step Financial Transfer task, the mechanism achieved a zero attack success rate and a zero false positive rate across state-of-the-art models.
For models that use LLM-as-the-Judge, the results are unstable.
Consequently, the verifier fundamentally proves the absence of violations against explicitly defined axioms, rather than the absence of unsafe behaviors.

extraction.framework: executable Proof-Constrained Action (ePCA)
extraction.topology: single untrusted LLM policy generator gated by a four-layer isolated verification plane (action proposal, deterministic translation, SMT formal verification, deterministic checking) acting as a reference monitor over the tool interface
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; two constructed environments - Scenario A, a controlled multi-step financial transfer task with time-segmentation and meta-rule attacks plus benign sequences, and Scenario B, an enterprise sandbox with a dual-zone network topology and five axioms, exercised through a 12-round data-exfiltration trajectory
extraction.baseline: Stateless Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) and empirical semantic guardrails implemented as LLM-as-a-Judge, both run across the same front-end models (GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-Max, Gemini 3.1 Flash, Kimi k2.5)
extraction.key_results: In Scenario A, ePCA reached 100.0% accuracy, 0.0% false-alarm rate and 100.0% F1 for every evaluated model; ABAC reached 50.0% accuracy / 66.7% F1 for four of five models and 98.3% / 99.2% for Gemini-3-flash; LLM-as-a-Judge ranged from 43.3% to 100.0% accuracy and 60.5% to 100.0% F1, with Claude-Sonnet 4.6 producing no valid executions; average decision latency 0.44 ms for ePCA versus 1.52e4 ms for the LLM judge and 1.10e-3 ms for ABAC. In Scenario B the 12-round exfiltration attempt was blocked by taint-lock axioms and the agent self-terminated after recognizing the deadlock.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the architecture relies on strongly typed schemas and static syntactic parsing, leaving it exposed to advanced schema-evasion attacks, while adding a neural parser would reintroduce probabilistic uncertainty; finite formal constraints cannot cover open, high-degree-of-freedom action spaces, so only critical operational paths are constrained; the axiom set is hard-coded from human expert modelling and scales poorly to multi-agent tasks with large dynamic state spaces; most fundamentally, the verifier proves absence of violations of explicitly defined axioms rather than absence of unsafe behaviour, so an omitted constraint yields a mathematically compliant but unsafe transition; empirical conclusions are limited to micro-benchmarking in controlled environments and the authors describe the experiments as illustrative realizations rather than statistically representative benchmarks; open, multi-tool and heterogeneous multi-agent evaluation is left to future work.

records.title: SARC: A Governance-by-Architecture Framework for Agentic AI Systems

evidence_notes.summary: SARC adds an explicit constraint primitive to the reinforcement-learning tuple and compiles each constraint declaration into one of four enforcement sites in the agent loop, with placement determined by constraint class (hard before dispatch, soft over completed actions, escalation through a router bounded by the action's reversibility window). For RQ1 the paper supplies both an argument and a caveat: it argues that prompt-layer guardrails cannot enforce hard constraints by construction because the model can route around them through tools whose effects are off-screen, and it proves that finite additive reward penalties cannot substitute for hard constraints when violations are low-probability and high-payoff. For RQ2 it runs a controlled comparison of five governance regimes over 50 seeds, and is notably careful about attribution - the 89.5% reduction in soft-window overages is credited to the declared throttling response being placed at the post-action auditor, not to the SARC label, and the authors state a policy-as-code system with the same response would perform similarly. The critical limitation for evidence quality is that the agent is a simulated procurement policy, not an LLM, so the results measure enforcement architecture rather than agent behaviour under instruction.

quotes.text: Prompt guardrails cannot enforce hard constraints by construction because the model may ignore, reinterpret, or route around them through tools whose effects are off-screen.
SARC reduces soft-window overages from ∼937 (policy-as-code-only) to98.8± 1.0, a89.5%reduction at95%confidence.

First, the environment is synthetic and intentionally stylized; results from a synthetic procurement task do not generalize to real procurement, customer-service, or clinical settings without further empirical work.

extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a synthetic procurement environment with 1,000 orders per episode over 50 random seeds, log-normal order amounts, one hard constraint (approval above EUR 50,000), one soft constraint (rolling 24-hour spend at or above EUR 475,000) and one escalation constraint (first-time supplier review), with a deliberately misaligned reward; artifacts released at github.com/besanson/sarc-governance
extraction.baseline: Four practitioner regimes: post-hoc audit, output filtering (modelled at 25% post-action coverage of the hard constraint), workflow rules (if/else gate before tool dispatch), and policy-as-code-only (hard constraint at the policy layer, escalation at the pre-action gate, no declared post-action throttling response)

Under a predicate-noise sweep, residual SARC violations rose from 0.00 at zero error to 3.66 +/- 0.59 per episode at predicate false-negative rate 0.10 and enforcement failure rate 0.05. The audit checker reported zero structural discrepancies across all 50 SARC seeds.
extraction.limitations: Authors state three threats to validity: the environment is synthetic and stylized and does not generalize to real procurement, customer-service or clinical settings; per-step latency figures are model parameters of each regime rather than measurements of any implementation; the reward is deliberately misaligned to expose the enforcement gap, and under a well-aligned reward the gap may narrow. They also state the evaluation does not show that SARC outperforms safe-RL training and includes no adversarial or indirect-prompt-injection testing; the zero-violation curve assumes exact predicates, active enforcement at every step and no bypass paths; the framework does not solve legal interpretation, predicate correctness, model reliability or organizational accountability; and state-dependent recursive call depth and out-of-trust-boundary market topologies in multi-agent settings are not formally characterized.

records.title: ProAgent: From Robotic Process Automation to Agentic Process Automation

evidence_notes.summary: This is the position-and-prototype paper that frames the RQ1 design space rather than testing it: it argues that rule-based RPA workflows are efficient but cannot handle dynamic decisions, while free-running LLM agents are flexible but inefficient, and proposes Agentic Process Automation as the hybrid. The concrete mechanism is an Agentic Workflow Description Language (JSON for data flow, Python for control flow) into which two agent node types are embedded: DataAgent for complex data processing and ControlAgent as a natural-language branch condition. This is the inverse of the RQ1 intervention: instead of constraining an agent with a process model, it relaxes a process model by inserting agents at the points that need judgement, which makes it useful for characterising where a binding process model must leave discretion. Evidence is a single GPT-4 proof-of-concept on the n8n platform (one commercial worksheet-routing task, a seven-node constructed workflow, two illustrated executions) with no metrics, no baseline and no compliance measurement, so it contributes vocabulary and an architecture to RQ2 but no empirical result. The authors' own safety discussion, that agents aggravate automation bias because humans transfer trust from deterministic workflows to hallucination-prone agents, is directly relevant to why explicit process binding is argued for.

records.title: Towards Enforcing Company Policy Adherence in Agentic Workflows

evidence_notes.summary: This is the closest direct test of RQ1 in the set: it holds the agent, tools and task fixed and swaps natural-language policy in the prompt for compiled, deterministic pre-conditions. An offline buildtime stage maps a free-form policy document onto the 14 tau-bench Airlines tools and generates executable ToolGuards via test-driven development; at runtime each guard runs immediately before its tool call and, on violation, blocks the call and returns the violated policy to the agent for revision. On the 22 tau-bench Airlines tasks whose user request violates policy, the prompt-only 'best-effort' baseline reaches pass^1 0.450 / pass^10 0.227, two reflection variants that re-inject the policy or the compact policy-tool mapping before each action move pass^10 only to 0.273, while the generated guards reach 0.685 / 0.500. That pattern is the key RQ1 signal: restating the same policy as natural language buys almost nothing, whereas compiling it into an executable precondition buys roughly twenty points, and the authors attribute the gain solely to the enforcement module since nothing else in the deployment changed. Crucially for RQ1's second half, the study measures the tau-bench pass metric (final database state versus annotated goal state), so compliance and task completion are scored together rather than traded off, though the guards only cover pre-invocation policies.

extraction.benchmark: tau-bench Airlines (22 of the 50 tasks in which the user request violates a policy); plus a 61-test suite (25 compliance, 36 violation) over the 6 state-mutating tools

records.title: Policy-Invisible Violations in LLM-Based Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This paper isolates the failure class that makes natural-language policy specification insufficient in principle: violations whose decisive facts (recipient status, document audience label, session scope) are absent from the agent-visible context, in a cooperative non-adversarial setting. It contributes PhantomPolicy (60 violation and 60 matched safe cases across eight categories, with all tool responses stripped of policy metadata) and Sentinel, an enforcement layer that translates each outbound tool call into proposed mutations of an organisational knowledge graph, forks and applies them speculatively, and checks seven declarative invariants to return Allow, Block or Clarify. Its most useful contribution to RQ1 is a three-way comparison on identical traces: no enforcement (risky-case violations in 54-59 of 60 cases per model), the same policy injected as high-level natural-language rules in the system prompt (violations drop from 95.3% to 40.7% but range from 25% to 85% across models), and world-state-grounded enforcement (92.99% accuracy, 92.71 F1, 5 false positives, 37 missed violations). The paper argues explicitly that prompt-level policy helps only when the model attends to the rules and is not a reliable compliance boundary, and its coverage-degradation experiment shows enforcement recall is bounded above by world-model coverage rather than invariant sophistication. records.title: MANTRA: Synthesizing SMT-Validated Compliance Benchmarks for Tool-Using LLM Agents

evidence_notes.summary: MANTRA addresses the measurement problem behind RQ1: how to decide, deterministically and at scale, whether an agent's tool-call trace actually followed a natural-language procedural manual. The pipeline chunks a manual into a dependence graph, samples subgraphs to control task difficulty, and then generates two artefacts independently from the same region: LLM-generated trace-level checks (required calls, forbidden calls, and after/before/follows/precedes ordering) and a symbolic world model expressed as a typed DSL of tool pre- and post-conditions. Both are compiled to bounded SMT and cross-validated with Z3 in forward (checks too weak) and backward (checks too strict) conflict searches, with an LLM repairing whichever artefact the conflicting trace implicates and human review only as a fallback. This is directly useful for RQ2 because it operationalises the process model as a state-transition system while the agent still receives only the natural-language manual, so the process model functions as an oracle rather than as a control. Its most quotable RQ1-adjacent finding is diagnostic: across 10,895 failed checks, 76% are missing required calls or missing ordering anchors and only 2% are pure ordering violations, meaning agents fail by skipping mandated gating reads before write-style tools rather than by misordering, and the model with a 0% premature-write rate on the tau2 domains is the one that leads them.

records.title: Evaluation of Automated Machinery Functional Safety Risk Assessment Using LLMs

evidence_notes.summary: This is not an agent study, but it is the cleanest controlled ablation in the set of the RQ1 contrast between an explicit decision model and unstructured natural language. The task is classifying the Required Performance Level from a free-text machinery hazard description; the explicit model is the ISO 13849-1 Annex A risk graph, injected verbatim into the prompt as deterministic S/F/P mapping rules, and the control is a zero-shot prompt containing only the hazard description and the expert role. Across 7,800 ISO 12100/13849-1 scenarios (stratified subsets of n=567 and n=100, temperature 0), zero-shot accuracy is 0.300-0.470 while rule-injected prompting reaches 0.990 for gpt-4.1-mini and 1.000 for deepseek-chat, a gain of over 50 percentage points that the authors attribute to structured input rather than model scale. Two secondary findings matter for RQ2: retrieval augmentation on top of the rules adds essentially nothing to accuracy but adds latency (up to 56.87s per sample for deepseek-chat), and the benefit of structured input is model-capacity-dependent, since llama3.2 never exceeds 0.410 even with the rules. The generalisation caveat for RQ1 is that this is single-turn classification with a deterministically computed ground truth and no tools, state mutation or task-completion dimension, so it cannot speak to the completion side of the RQ1 trade-off. The text file quotes the authors' own prompt templates (for example a system message casting the model as a machinery safety expert); these are experimental artefacts reported as data and were treated as such.

records.title: Comparing Generative Chatbots Based on Process Requirements: A Case Study

evidence_notes.summary: This case study tests the weakest possible form of the RQ1 intervention: hand the LLM the BPMN XML of a process model, tell it to act as an agent honouring BPMN restrictions, and see whether the model constrains behaviour when no process engine enforces it. Thirteen evaluation questions cover start events, forward flow, history, end events, decision points and unintended paths on a single Trip Planning model built in Camunda Modeler. GPT-3.5 met 92.31% of the questions and PaLM 2 only 69.23%, but the two failure modes are identical and are exactly the ones RQ1 cares about: both models let the user execute a task that was not yet enabled (EQ12 not met), and both only partially handled the exclusive gateway, with GPT presenting the gateway itself as a task and PaLM listing both outgoing branches and then silently inferring the user's choice. The finding is that a formal process model supplied as prompt context conveys structure well enough for the model to recall history and explain gateway conditions, but does not produce enforcement: the model fabricates state (assuming an unperformed task was done) and admits unreachable tasks. That supports treating in-context process models as guidance rather than as a control mechanism, and motivates the external-guard designs seen elsewhere in this batch. Evidence is one process model, three BPMN construct types and two models, all qualitatively scored by the authors.

records.title: Enhancing declarative business process management availability through generative AI

evidence_notes.summary: This paper is upstream of RQ1: rather than binding an agent to a process model, it uses LLMs to manufacture the process models themselves, addressing the scarcity of multi-perspective declarative (MP-Declare) models caused by commercial confidentiality. Terpsichora combines role-play prompting, knowledge injection and few-shot examples with two constrained-generation mechanisms, Function Calling and Structured Output, over a Pydantic metamodel that enforces MP-Declare syntax, plus a validation loop that regenerates on failure and a Declare4Py-based check. Its relevance to RQ1 is the empirical contrast between constraint mechanisms rather than between constrained and unconstrained generation: Structured Output, which enforces a JSON schema, produced far richer conditional logic (mean 2.59 activation and 2.25 correlation conditions versus 0.20 and 0.01 for Function Calling on GPT-4o) and held labelling-convention compliance as complexity rose, whereas Function Calling gave more predictable structure but degraded. For RQ2 it supplies the declarative side of the control-mechanism vocabulary, since declarative models constrain by prohibition rather than by prescribing a sequence, which is the alternative to the imperative binding RQ1 assumes. The evaluation is of artefact quality (complexity metrics, label conventions, rediscovery from generated logs), not of any agent's compliance behaviour, so it contributes no violation or completion data.

records.title: PolicyFaultBench: Mutation-Based Assurance of Policy Mediation and Proposal-Interface Conformance for Tool- Using AI Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This paper deliberately removes the agent's planning freedom in order to test the control mechanism itself: the prompt supplies a frozen synthetic operation so the model merely transcribes it, and what is measured is whether the deterministic fail-closed mediator between proposal and side effect authorises correctly. Its distinctive contribution to RQ2 is turning the policy into an object of assurance rather than a trusted given, by applying twelve first-order mutation operators (subject widening, approval-gate bypass, temporal-constraint deletion, fail-open exception, state-reset omission and others) to two independently implemented policy architectures, an ordered-rule engine and a capability engine. The frozen 40-case corpus killed only 7 of 12 ordered-rule mutants, and an externally derived AgentDojo corpus killed just 2 of 12, showing that a corpus can produce high execution success while being weak at exposing policy faults; survivor-guided probes closed the gap but are labelled as repair rather than independent validation. A second result relevant to RQ1's completion side is that strictness costs availability without costing safety: nine benign Anthropic proposals were quarantined purely for adding an unrequested approval-scope annotation, breaking the preregistered 800/800 rule while every admitted proposal agreed under both policies and no containment failure occurred. The authors are explicit that this design cannot support claims about autonomous tool selection or planning under untrusted content.

records.title: FRAMES: Guarded and Dual-Objective Skill Evolution for Agents in Policy-Governed Enterprise Workflows

evidence_notes.summary: This is the strongest RQ1 evidence in my batch: it directly contrasts an agent given the policy as natural-language instructions in its prompt (B1 Raw LLM) against the same agent bound to explicit, structured, step-ordered skill procedures derived from the same policy, on a deployed financial document-auditing system and on tau-bench. extraction.framework: FRAMES (Feedback-driven Reasoning with Adaptive Mutation and Evolution of Skills)
extraction.topology: offline evolution pipeline with a population of parallel diagnosers feeding a consolidator and a skill rewriter, plus a single policy agent executing skills at serving time
extraction.benchmark: FinDAS internal production financial document-auditing cases (disjoint 210-case evolution set and 210-case held-out test set, 70 each of general, hallucination, special) plus the public tau-bench retail (110 cases) and airline (50 cases) domains
extraction.baseline: B1 Raw LLM with policies supplied in the prompt and no skill bank; B2 LLM-converted skills; B3 human-reviewed and edited skills; B4 single batch update; B5 AutoSkill (prior skill-evolution method)
extraction.key_results: On the held-out FinDAS test set (pass@k, k=3) total pass rates were Raw LLM 0.21, LLM skills 0.23, Human skills 0.60, Batch update 0.66, AutoSkill 0.71 and FRAMES 0.80; the prompt-only and LLM-skill baselines scored 0.04 on hallucination and 0.00 on special cases while FRAMES reached 0.86 general, 0.91 hallucination and 0.63 special. FRAMES led the strongest baseline in every category by 0.07-0.11, with paired bootstrap 95% CI [+0.038,+0.148] and McNemar exact p=0.0026 (28 of 37 discordant cases won by FRAMES). On tau-bench, FRAMES scored 0.98 total on retail (tied with batch update) and 0.96 on airline versus 0.92 for the strongest baseline, reaching 1.00 on airline hallucination versus 0.86. FRAMES also posted the lowest output-token cost (4.06k per case versus 6.48k for AutoSkill).
extraction.limitations: Authors state that no public benchmark tests what FRAMES targets, so evaluation rests on anonymised internal production cases plus a tau-bench adaptation offering few cases. Gains scale with feedback quality and shrink under sparse or noisy signal. Because the model is frozen and only skills are edited, capabilities the base model lacks cannot be added. Re-scoring every case through full agent runs makes evaluation one to two orders of magnitude costlier than all other modules, currently capping the loop at a few hundred cases. They also flag residual algorithmic-bias risk requiring ongoing demographic audits.

records.title: Enhancing Trust in LLM-Based AI Automation Agents: New Considerations and Future Challenges

evidence_notes.summary: An early workshop position paper that ports trust constructs from human-to-human and human-automation research (reliability, openness, tangibility, immediacy, task characteristics, trust trajectory) onto LLM-based business process automation agents. Its RQ2 value is a named catalogue of control considerations rather than results: prompt mediation, content and output mediation, task grounding, knowledge grounding, application grounding, user feedback, pre-deployment testing in a dev mode, safety guardrails and graceful failure. It also draws the distinction RQ1 depends on operationally, separating human-in-the-loop moderated actions from autonomous actions that alter the business without supervision, and flags open-ended tasks with no completion criterion as the hardest trust case. The assessment section is a subjective four-product comparison (ChatGPT+plugins, MS Copilot, AgentGPT, Adept.ai) scored yes/no/unknown by the authors, with no measurement, no task set and no violation counts. The authors themselves call it not a detailed comparison and note that testing tooling was absent from the products they examined.

quotes.text:

with a high degree of accuracy.

influence the business without any human supervision.

We note that this is not a detailed comparison and might not reflect
the entire abilities of the tools but rather our own opinion after trying these models.

extraction.topology: n/a (notes that complex tasks involve multiple agents or skills whose outputs must be aggregated, but specifies no topology)
extraction.key_results: No quantitative results. The paper reports a qualitative yes/no/unknown assessment of four products across reliability (mediation, grounding, feedback, testing), openness (reliability, goal, algorithm), tangibility, immediacy, task characteristics and trust trajectory; notably all four products were rated as lacking pre-execution testing support, and only ChatGPT+plugins was rated positively on mediation, grounding and feedback.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the product comparison is not detailed, may not reflect the full abilities of the tools, and reflects their own opinion after trying the models. Ethics/legal and style-adaptation dimensions were excluded because they were difficult to assess, and prompt/output mediation and the grounding considerations were merged for presentation. They also state that no overall metric framework for trust in LLM-based automation agents yet exists and call for new testing and validation methodologies.

records.title: Real-Time Regulatory Intelligence Framework: LLM-powered compliance automation for financial services

evidence_notes.summary: Proposes a five-layer architecture (ingestion, processing, LLM interpretation, policy orchestration, human-in-the-loop governance) that turns financial regulatory text into infrastructure-as-code controls, and reports many performance figures against manual and rule-based compliance. For RQ1 the useful signal is directional rather than evidential: the paper repeatedly reports that prescriptive, rules-based provisions are interpreted far more accurately than principle-based provisions requiring contextual interpretation, which is consistent with the hypothesis that explicit structure helps most where the policy is already determinate. For RQ2 I would not count this as an empirical evaluation: no experimental protocol, sample construction, model identity, statistical test, code or data is given, the reported numbers are attributed inline to third-party references including vendor blogs, and headline figures are mutually inconsistent across sections (94.2% versus 94.7% interpretation accuracy; time-to-compliance 64.3 to 7.8 days versus 63.7 to 7.2 days). This is a compliance-interpretation pipeline rather than an agent bound to a process model, so it speaks to RQ1 only by analogy. I have recorded its claims verbatim without endorsing them.

extraction.topology: n/a (layered microservices pipeline with event-driven communication; no autonomous agents described)
extraction.benchmark: an author-described benchmark dataset of 8,750 annotated regulatory provisions, plus domain case studies over 12,478 suspicious-activity-report requirements, 8,923 prudential control provisions and 6,347 consumer-protection requirements; none of these datasets is publicly identified or released

records.title: Agentic AI for Regulatory Intelligence: Designing Scalable Compliance Lifecycle Systems in Multinational Tech Enterprises

evidence_notes.summary: A narrative review that proposes a multi-agent compliance lifecycle architecture in which specialised agents handle horizon scanning, risk scoring, control mapping and remediation under a coordinator, with sentinel agents supervising peers and federated edge deployment for data sovereignty. For RQ2 its most transferable idea is an externalised control layer: Governance-as-a-Service that intercepts agent actions, evaluates them against declarative rules, assigns trust scores and modulates behaviour without modifying agent internals, which is architecturally the inverse of embedding policy in the prompt. It also usefully cites the compliance-monitoring literature to argue that most deployed monitoring is reactive and binary, and that predictive monitoring quantifying distance from compliance boundaries is preferable. For RQ1 it offers no evidence: there is no experiment, no benchmark, no baseline and no measurement, the Amazon 'case study' is inferred from public sources with hedged language rather than primary data, and the review states no search protocol or inclusion criteria. Best treated as a source of control-mechanism vocabulary and of stated risks (algorithmic overreach, ambiguous liability, regulatory capture) rather than as evidence.

records.title: OpenMCPSpec: A Specification Framework for Robust, Governed, and Lifecycle-Managed Machine Communicable Processes in LLM-Agent Systems

evidence_notes.summary: Proposes an extended Model Context Protocol schema that moves governance metadata (pii, gdpr_sensitive, roles), reliability hints (nlp_hints) and lifecycle/versioning information out of middleware and into the machine-readable tool contract, so that policy can be enforced at the binding layer before business logic runs. This is a close structural analogue of RQ1 at the tool-call level: the declared baseline is a zero-shot prompt carrying only basic tool descriptions, and the treatment is the same tools bound to an explicit specification. The governance result is the striking one for RQ1's violation side: nine of ten policy rules leaked without the specification and passed with it, with only metadata integrity passing in both conditions. The reliability side is much weaker evidence: only twenty tests in total on a single SQLite MCP server with one model, and the ACI metric is defined in the text as a relative accuracy improvement while the results table actually reports execution times in seconds, so the reported gains measure latency rather than argument correctness. The authors themselves report one negative case where hints over-constrained the model on an open-ended task.

extraction.framework: OpenMCPSpec (extended Model Context Protocol schema with embedded governance, nlp_hints and lifecycle metadata; open-source schema and Python reference implementation)
extraction.topology: single agent invoking tools on an MCP server through a specification binding layer that intercepts and validates calls before business logic executes
extraction.benchmark: ad hoc: 20 tests total (10 ACI, 10 CPR) against a SQLite MCP server using qwen3-coder:480b-cloud via a free cloud Ollama API; schema, spec and test scripts published on GitHub
extraction.baseline: a standard zero-shot prompt containing only basic tool descriptions and parameter names (basic MCP), compared against the same setup with the nlp_hints array injected and governance metadata enforced
extraction.key_results: Across the 10 ACI tests, nine showed gains ranging from +11.4% to +38.7% and one (Semantic Summary) regressed by -23.7%; the authors report an independent two-sample t-test giving p<0.05 across the optimized categories. Note the reported ACI table columns are execution times in seconds (baseline 1.996-3.110s versus OpenMCP 1.591-2.598s), not argument-correctness rates as the metric definition states. On the 10 CPR governance rules, nine (pattern refusal, RBAC scope, PII protection, SQL injection, field RBAC, missing audit ID, rate limit, geo-fence, policy violation) are recorded as FAIL (Leaked) without the spec and PASS (Compliant) with it, while metadata integrity passed in both conditions.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that strict nlp_hints over-constrain the LLM on inherently broad tasks and are optimal for deterministic parameter mapping rather than open-ended generation, and that mandating complex JSON schema validation introduces marginal parsing overhead at the orchestration layer. The roadmap concedes that advanced parameter constraints, standardised error schemas and testing-tooling integration are not yet part of the schema. The authors do not discuss the very small sample (20 tests, one model, one MCP server) as a limitation.
